It's an "awesome" security measure that was introduced to replace / enhance the system BIOS a while back. As to how it can cause issues for you, it will prevent anything from booting that isn't signed by a list of pre-authorized keys; namely, keys that have been given Microsoft's blessing. Thankfully, most Linux distros have managed to get their keys signed because Microsoft doesn't want another anti-trust lawsuit just yet, but I digress...

You said you're using Mint? I presume it's version 17.2? If so, you're good on the UEFI front. Personally, I turn that crap off because it only causes issues booting things, but if you already have a boot loader installed with UEFI enabled, you should leave it turned on. Tricksy, innit?

If you've already got a successful Mint install on what is effectively /dev/sda3, then all you have to do is install the grub boot loader and give it a proper config. You can do this from the Mint LiveCD. Once it boots, open a terminal window and do the following (hashes are my comments, don't type them):

I can't remember if the LiveCD gives you a root terminal, so become root

sudo bash

Mount your Linux partition to /mnt

mount /dev/sda3 /mnt

We need some filesystems from the LiveCD mounted under there, so...

mount --bind /proc /mnt/proc
mount --bind /dev /mnt/dev
mount --bind /sys /mnt/sys

Now we're setting your Linux install as the root filesystem for the grub install

chroot /mnt

Let's do this...

grub-install /dev/sda
update-grub

You're done. You should see some stuff here about what operating systems it detected. You can close out the terminal now. After that, you can reboot the system, pop out the disc, and you should be greeted with a configured grub menu.

Quick question: It automatically loads linux (which I prefer, it's perfect), but how do I boot into windows? Can I just do the del/F11 on startup?

Looking at it now, it looks like Mint's grub config is set to hide the menu from you. Otherwise you'd get a nice menu to let you choose which OS you want to boot. You could either bang the arrow keys right after POST, as the machine is booting, to bring up the grub menu, or you can edit the menu to make it stop being hidden. To do the latter, open /etc/default/grub as root and comment out the two lines with "HIDDEN" in them:

sudo gedit /etc/default/grub

Find the two lines that start with "GRUB_HIDDEN" and place a has mark in front of them, then save and close the file. After that, you need to tell grub to rewrite its config file using the new settings:

sudo update-grub

And that should do it. Next time you reboot, you should get a menu for ten seconds. That file also has the place to adjust the time for the menu, so play around with that if ten seconds ends up being too annoying -- most people stick with three or so.

I'm still on Win7, and plan to keep a Win7 installation until it either stops being compatible with my hardware, or until 400 of my Steam games get ported to Linux. But, given that Windows stopped being good after Windows 7, the Windows 10 debacle just makes this seem like a good time to transition to Linux. I'm debating between dual-booting alongside either Debian, or OpenSUSE.

Debian is obviously a solid choice, being the basis for Mint, Ubuntu, and SteamOS. It's a very basic, minimal Linux installation, and certainly one of the most widely supported. I'm vaguely familiar with apt-get, so that's a plus, and most of the commands I pick up on my desktop or Raspberry Pi(running Raspbian) would be usable on the other device.

OpenSUSE has also been one of the popular choices for a great many years, and I've heard many great things about it... None of which I understand, not being familiar with Linux. Something about YaST making configuring things easier, and Open Build Service making updates easier. It also uses KDE by default, which, while not of major importance due to ease of just installing a different desktop environment, certainly isn't a downside.

I'm kind of biased to go towards Debian, just because I know that's a safe choice, but I've also heard and read enough good things about OpenSUSE to know that it sounds like a really solid choice. What do you guys think about the matter?
Come time for my SSD upgrade, I'm going to dual-boot and start transitioning away from Win7. Should I go with OpenSUSE or Debian?

I'm not too familiar with OpenSUSE or YaST, but easy configuration generally means that there's lots of graphical tools for editing config files you could just as well edit directly. If you don't mind such tools and if you like KDE, I suppose you could go for either distro. My personal preferance would be Debian, but my only real complaint against OpenSUSE is that it's heavy and comes with a lot of stuff I don't need.

One good thing about Debian is that if you run into a problem, the solutions you''ll find on Ubuntu or Mint forums will mostly be directly applicable.
Debian is a great, solid distro. I know that OpenSuse is pretty good as a desktop distro though.

Debian doesn't really try and be easy, it tries to be right. Ubuntu is Debian with extras added to be easy. I however still recommend SUSE for desktop use. It's actually made with desktop use in mind and comes with convince features, Yast means not having to manually make changes. It also doesn't criticize 3rd party software, SUSE will officially install Steam with only a small disclaimer.
